newsitem.title: GERMANY: German steel workers down tools to defend jobs.
newsitem.headline: German steel workers down tools to defend jobs.

text.p: Germany's major steelworks were idle Wednesday after unions vowed to fight the creation of a joint venture between steel giants Krupp and Thyssen that could cost 8,000 jobs.

Thousands of steel workers clad in white fire-proof overalls demonstrated at the Krupp Hoesch Stahl works in Dortmund against a job cuts plan presented to the works council at a meeting with company officials late Tuesday.

Workers at the Thyssen Stahl plant in Duisburg also refused to go to work, continuing a week of stoppages since Fried. Krupp AG Hoesch-Krupp last week launched a hostile takeover bid for much larger rival steel group Thyssen AG.
Krupp dropped the bid after five days of talks with Thyssen in which the firms agreed to form a steel joint venture, hammering out the details over the next four weeks.
But this did not cool the tempers of workers fearing job losses in Germany's already depressed coal and steel heartland.

"If the companies need four weeks, then so do we," Juergen Hafner, chairman of the workers' council at the Krupp Hoesch Stahl plant, said late Tuesday after being briefed by Krupp management and deciding to continue the work stoppages.

Harald Schartau, head of the North Rhine-Westphalia arm of powerful steel and engineering union IG Metall, said the union would provide "massive resistance" to protest the restructuring moves. After being informed of plans for the alliance, he said it would cost as many as 8,000 jobs over four to five years.
Many of the cuts would come at Krupp Hoesch Stahl, itself the product of a 1991 merger between Krupp and rival Hoesch AG, where blast furnace operations in Dortmund would be shut down.
Thyssen Stahl chairman Ekkehard Schulz was due to address steel workers at a gathering of employees later on Wednesday and outline the restructuring plans.

Hans-Wilhelm Grasshoff, the chief of Krupp's steel operation, told a workers meeting late Tuesday that Thyssen would take a 60 percent share in the venture. The joint company will be founded on April 1, but production in the two companies' steel units is likely to continue as before until mid to late 1998, he said.

Thyssen AG chief executive Dieter Vogel said the consequences of a hostile takeover "would have been far worse than what will happen now that Thyssen will steer the fusion." Speaking on German television he said Thyssen's steel operations, unlike Krupp's, were competitive even without the merger, but that the compromise was a "victory for reason."
But so far the workers have not been convinced.
